limitations: The authors state the overall survival pattern raises the possibility that a LARGER study would show equivocal R1 to be an intermediate prognostic group, and that larger studies are needed to settle this definitively
They argue sub-categorisation of R1 could be supported only if a clear distinction between the two R1 groups were evident, which these data do not show
Involvement of the anterior pancreatic surface, excluded from the R1 definition here, could potentially affect survival
Histological data were incomplete for a small number of cases, so the multivariable model included 155 of 163 patients
Meaningful comparison of R1 rates between centres is complicated by the lack of standardised margin terminology and of any internationally recognised pathology protocol
critique: THE CONCLUSION IS DRAWN FROM A NON-SIGNIFICANT TEST, WHICH IS AN ARGUMENT FROM ABSENCE OF EVIDENCE. 'No significant difference' between 57 and 71 patients (P=0.102) in a cohort with 13.9-month median survival cannot establish equivalence; the medians differ by 2.8 months and the point estimates sit between the R0 and unequivocal-R1 groups exactly as an intermediate category would. The authors concede this in the discussion but the abstract concludes the two should be 'considered synonymous'

THE COMPARISON THE RULE ACTUALLY NEEDS IS EQUIVOCAL R1 VERSUS R0, AND THAT WAS ALSO NON-SIGNIFICANT (P=0.114). The study therefore cannot distinguish equivocal R1 from either neighbour, which is a statement about power, not biology, in a cohort of only 35 R0 patients

SINGLE CENTRE, SINGLE PATHOLOGIST, RETROSPECTIVE. One consultant pathologist re-reviewed only the R0 cases, so the reclassification effort was applied asymmetrically - cases already called R1 were not re-examined for over-calling, which is the direction of error that would inflate the 79% figure

ONLY 35 R0 PATIENTS DEFINE THE REFERENCE GROUP, and their median survival of 25.4 months has a 95% CI of 10.5-40.8 months - a four-fold range. Every comparison in the paper is anchored to this unstable estimate

THE 1997-2007 ERA MEANS ONLY 27% RECEIVED ADJUVANT CHEMOTHERAPY, at a time when ESPAC-1 and CONKO-001 were establishing it. Margin status interacts with adjuvant therapy, and a cohort in which three quarters got no chemotherapy cannot speak to the prognostic weight of R1 in a modern pathway

MARGIN STATUS DID NOT SURVIVE MULTIVARIABLE ADJUSTMENT, which undercuts the premise that getting the R1 definition right matters prognostically. The paper treats this as a technical problem (collinearity with tumour size) rather than as evidence that margin status may be a marker of tumour burden rather than an independent determinant of outcome

THE DECISION TO EXCLUDE THE ANTERIOR SURFACE, PanIN-3, PERINEURAL AND NODAL INVOLVEMENT FROM THE R1 DEFINITION IS A SERIES OF CONVENTIONS, NOT FINDINGS. Different centres make different choices, and the paper's own argument - that the 79% rate reflects pathology protocol rather than surgical quality - applies equally to its own conventions

THE MOST IMPORTANT IMPLICATION FOR A PATHWAY IS NOT THE ONE THE PAPER EMPHASISES. If the <1 mm rule moves the R1 rate from 44% to 79% at one centre, then R0 and R1 rates reported in every neoadjuvant and adjuvant trial are a function of local pathology practice. PREOPANC (R0 71% of resected under RCPath <1 mm), ESPAC-5 (R0 14-23%), NORPACT-1 (R0 56% vs 39%) and APACT (no central pathology review, R0 76%) are not comparable to each other, and no trial in this depot reports a pathology quality-assurance measure comparable to the one described here except ESPAC5 and CONKO-007

The argument that R1 is under-reported because 60-80% of resected patients recur locally is an indirect inference: local recurrence can arise from biologically aggressive residual disease beyond any resectable margin, not only from microscopic margin positivity

Funded by Cancer Research UK with no declared conflicts, and the senior authors are the ESPAC trialists who went on to apply this definition in ESPAC-4 and ESPAC-5 - a coherent programme, but the definition and the trials that use it come from the same group
19723142.n: 163 pancreatoduodenectomy specimens; 128 R1 (79%), of which 57 (45% of R1) equivocal and 71 unequivocal; 35 R0
19723142.bottom_line: This single-centre study of 163 pancreatoduodenectomies supplied the only clinical evidence for the <1 mm R1 rule by showing that 'equivocal' R1 survival (15.4 months) resembles unequivocal R1 (12.6 months) more than R0 (25.4 months), and that the rule raises the R1 rate from 44% to 79% - but the key comparison was non-significant in a small cohort, margin status did not survive multivariable adjustment, and the real lesson is that R0 rates reported across pancreatic trials are largely a function of pathology protocol.
19723142.funding: Supported by Cancer Research UK. No conflicts of interest are declared.

limitations: The authors note the optimal duration of biliary drainage before surgery has not been established, with experimental and clinical data suggesting at least 4-6 weeks is needed
Earlier randomised studies used percutaneous rather than endoscopic drainage, which the authors invoke to explain why their hospital stay result differs from previous trials
Older trials mixed proximal and distal bile-duct obstruction, now regarded as different diseases needing different treatment

The authors explicitly flag that with the advent of neoadjuvant chemotherapy the question becomes clinically relevant again, and that given their poor results with PLASTIC stents, drainage during neoadjuvant treatment might be better achieved with METAL stents, which have higher patency and do not affect surgical outcome
critique: COMPARATOR: surgery within one week of diagnosis, which required dedicated operating-room capacity guaranteed by all 13 hospitals specifically for the trial. This is the key external-validity problem: the control strategy is only available where a jaundiced patient can be operated on within seven days. A pathway that cannot deliver that has not got the comparator the trial tested, and delay without drainage is not what was studied

PLASTIC STENTS ONLY - AND THE AUTHORS SAY THIS IS THE PROBLEM. The 26% cholangitis and 30% stent-exchange rates are largely properties of plastic endoprostheses over 4-6 weeks. Self-expanding metal stents, which every neoadjuvant protocol in this depot (PREOPANC, PREOPANC-2, NORPACT-1, ESPAC5) specifies or prefers, were not tested. Citing this trial against biliary drainage before neoadjuvant chemotherapy is citing it outside its evidence

NEOADJUVANT CHEMOTHERAPY WAS AN EXCLUSION CRITERION, so the trial has nothing to say about the situation in which drainage is now most often needed - bridging a jaundiced patient through months of chemotherapy. NORPACT-1 stented 57% of its neoadjuvant arm and had 2 patients derailed by persistent jaundice; PREOPANC had 10 patients whose treatment was delayed by it. That is the modern question and this trial predates it

NON-RECEIPT AND CROSSOVER: 6/202 were excluded after randomisation (2 withdrew consent, 4 had out-of-range bilirubin). Two early-surgery patients had their operation cancelled and 7 drainage patients never reached surgery. Two early-surgery patients nonetheless had drainage-related complications, implying some crossover to stenting before operation

THE PRIMARY OUTCOME COUNTS DRAINAGE COMPLICATIONS AND SURGICAL COMPLICATIONS IN ONE TOTAL, WHICH GUARANTEES THE RESULT. A strategy with an extra procedure will have extra procedural complications; the informative question is whether drainage made the OPERATION safer, and on that the trial is null (RR 0.79, CI 0.57-1.11). The 39%-versus-74% headline is therefore partly definitional, and the trial is underpowered for the surgical-complication comparison it was designed around

DESIGNED FOR NON-INFERIORITY WITH A 10-PERCENTAGE-POINT MARGIN AND 94 PATIENTS PER ARM, assuming complication rates of 38% and 48%. The observed 74% in the drainage arm far exceeded the assumption, so the trial is well powered for its headline but not for mortality (CI 0.42-1.72), resection rate (P=0.11) or surgical complications

BILIRUBIN WAS CAPPED AT 250 micromol/L, excluding the most deeply jaundiced patients - exactly those in whom drainage is most often considered unavoidable. PREOPANC used 250 micromol/L as the threshold ABOVE which it recommended drainage, so the two trials address non-overlapping populations

FIFTEEN OF 196 PATIENTS (8%) DID NOT HAVE ADENOCARCINOMA, including 5 with chronic pancreatitis and 3 with stones, and they remain in the analysis - a reminder that the preoperative diagnosis is wrong in roughly one in twelve jaundiced patients taken to pancreatoduodenectomy

THE 7% OVERALL MORTALITY IS HIGH for centres performing at least 10 resections a year and is presented as acceptable because it did not differ between arms; the authors use it to argue for centralisation, but it also means the trial's complication rates come from an era and a volume standard below modern expectations

Complications were adjudicated blind, which is a real strength, but the treating teams and patients were unblinded and readmission decisions - the outcome with the largest relative difference - are clinician-dependent
20071702.n: 202 randomised, 196 analysed (94 early surgery, 102 biliary drainage); 120 resections
20071702.bottom_line: The DROP trial showed that routinely draining the bile duct with a plastic stent for 4-6 weeks before pancreatoduodenectomy nearly doubles serious complications (74% vs 39%, RR 0.54) without reducing surgical complications or mortality, so surgery within a week is preferable when it can be delivered - but it used plastic stents only, capped bilirubin at 250 micromol/L and excluded neoadjuvant chemotherapy, so it does not settle how to manage jaundice during months of preoperative treatment.
20071702.funding: Netherlands Organization for Health Research and Development, which had no access to outcome data during the trial and did not participate in analysis or manuscript preparation. No endoscopic equipment or stents were donated by manufacturers. Two authors report lecture fees from Boston Scientific and consulting or lecture fees from GI Dynamics, Covidien and Johnson & Johnson.

limitations: No separate limitations section; the authors frame their own eligibility criteria as the boundary of applicability, concluding FOLFIRINOX is an option for patients under 76 with ECOG 0-1, no cardiac ischaemia and normal or near-normal bilirubin
There were fewer measurable lung metastases in the FOLFIRINOX group (19.5% vs 28.7%, P=0.05), and the authors state results were similar when adjusted for pulmonary metastases
Filgrastim was not recommended as primary prophylaxis but could be used for high-risk patients, which the authors note in describing the toxicity profile
critique: The paper has no limitations section, so every point below is unstated

COMPARATOR: single-agent gemcitabine, which was the genuine standard of care in 2005-2009 - one of the few trials in this depot whose comparator was appropriate at the time it ran. Nothing in the trial addresses adjuvant or neoadjuvant use, yet PRODIGE-24, NORPACT-1, PREOPANC-2, SWOG S1505 and A021501 all justify their regimen by extrapolating from this metastatic result, an extrapolation PREOPANC-2 explicitly shows does not hold

NON-RECEIPT OF ALLOCATED TREATMENT: 4/171 in the FOLFIRINOX arm and 2/171 in the gemcitabine arm never received treatment (safety populations of 167 and 169), and 8 and 7 patients had minor eligibility violations. Non-receipt was minimal and balanced - a genuine strength

THE POPULATION IS NARROW AND THE PAPER'S OWN CONCLUSION SAYS SO: age under 76, ECOG 0-1, no cardiac disease, bilirubin at or below 1.5x normal, no chronic diarrhoea, MEASURABLE disease. MPACT, run concurrently, included patients up to 88 and 8% with ECOG 2 equivalent. Real-world metastatic PDAC populations are older, frailer and frequently jaundiced; the 11.1-month median is not their expectation

PHASE 2 AND PHASE 3 PATIENTS WERE POOLED. The 88 phase 2 patients, enrolled at 15 centres under a response-rate endpoint, are included in the phase 3 survival analysis. The trial was continued only because the phase 2 response gate was met, so the pooled estimate incorporates a selection step conditional on early efficacy

THE QUALITY-OF-LIFE RESULT IS THE MOST SURPRISING AND LEAST SCRUTINISED FINDING. Time to definitive deterioration is a time-to-event endpoint in which patients who die or progress stop contributing; a regimen that delays progression by 3.1 months will delay quality-of-life deterioration almost mechanically. Interpreting 31% versus 66% as showing FOLFIRINOX improves quality of life despite far worse toxicity requires assuming the deterioration measure is independent of survival, which it is not

THE TOXICITY COMPARISON IS NOT LIKE FOR LIKE ON SUPPORTIVE CARE: 42.5% of FOLFIRINOX patients received filgrastim versus 5.3% of gemcitabine patients, so the observed 45.7% grade 3-4 neutropenia rate is already a growth-factor-supported figure, and the exposure differed two-fold (10 vs 6 cycles), meaning the FOLFIRINOX arm had more time at risk for cumulative toxicity

SUBSEQUENT THERAPY CROSSED OVER HEAVILY AND ASYMMETRICALLY: 82.5% of FOLFIRINOX patients got gemcitabine afterwards and about half of gemcitabine patients got an oxaliplatin-based regimen. Post-second-line survival was identical at 4.4 months in both arms, so the 4.3-month difference reflects first-line sequencing rather than any effect unique to the four-drug combination
BASELINE IMBALANCE IN LUNG METASTASES FAVOURED FOLFIRINOX (19.4% vs 28.7%, P=0.05), acknowledged and adjusted for, but in a 342-patient trial other unmeasured imbalances cannot be excluded

RELATIVE DOSE INTENSITY OF 78-82% MEANS THE REGIMEN AS DELIVERED WAS ALREADY DOSE-ATTENUATED, which is part of why the later 'modified' FOLFIRINOX (no bolus, lower irinotecan) performs similarly; the trial does not establish that full-dose FOLFIRINOX is necessary

Oxaliplatin and irinotecan were DONATED by Sanofi-Aventis and Pfizer and the trial received grants from Amgen (maker of filgrastim, used in 42.5% of the experimental arm); the manufacturers are stated to have had no role in design, accrual, analysis or writing, and writing assistance came from the sponsor Unicancer and a medical communications company
21561347.n: 342 patients (171 per arm by ITT; safety population 167 and 169); 273 deaths (79.8%)
21561347.bottom_line: PRODIGE 4/ACCORD 11 established FOLFIRINOX as first-line therapy for metastatic pancreatic cancer, raising median survival from 6.8 to 11.1 months (HR 0.57) and delaying quality-of-life deterioration despite markedly more neutropenia, diarrhoea and neuropathy - but only in patients under 76 with ECOG 0-1, no cardiac disease and near-normal bilirubin, with heavy crossover to the other regimen at progression, and it provides no evidence for FOLFIRINOX in the neoadjuvant or adjuvant setting.
21561347.funding: Clinical Research Hospital Program grants (PHRC 2004 and 2007) from the French Ministry of Health, grants from Amgen, and the French National League against Cancer. Oxaliplatin and irinotecan were donated by Sanofi-Aventis and Pfizer, stated to have had no role in design, accrual, analysis or manuscript preparation. Writing assistance was provided by an employee of the sponsor (Unicancer) and by Miller Medical Communications. Several authors report advisory board and lecture fees from Pfizer, Sanofi-Aventis, Roche, Amgen, Bayer, Merck and Novartis.

limitations: The authors note that, given the high relapse rate in the first year and the fact that gemcitabine was standard therapy at relapse, the design can be seen as a study of IMMEDIATE versus DELAYED postoperative gemcitabine rather than of chemotherapy versus none
The trial was community-based without uniform surgical standards and without centralised pathology review; the authors frame this as generalisability rather than a weakness
Subgroup analyses were predefined but exploratory with limited power
Overall survival was a secondary endpoint; the trial was powered on disease-free survival
critique: COMPARATOR: THE CONTROL ARM RECEIVED NO ADJUVANT TREATMENT AT ALL - observation only. This makes CONKO-001 the foundation of adjuvant therapy but also means it says nothing about any modern regimen; every later trial measures against gemcitabine, which this trial only establishes as better than nothing

NON-RECEIPT OF ALLOCATED TREATMENT: 18/186 (10%) randomised to gemcitabine never started it, mostly because of postoperative complications and wound-healing problems, and only 111/186 (62%) completed all six cycles. The observation arm by definition had no treatment to fail to receive, so non-receipt is entirely one-sided and biases the ITT comparison TOWARD the null - a point in the trial's favour

THE ELIGIBILITY CRITERION OF POSTOPERATIVE CA19-9 BELOW 2.5x NORMAL (about 92.5 kU/L) SILENTLY EXCLUDED THE WORST-PROGNOSIS PATIENTS. ESPAC-4 later showed that the 17% of resected patients with CA19-9 above 92.5 kU/L have a median survival of 13.1 months versus 29.6 months below it. CONKO-001's survival curves therefore describe a favourably selected population, and its 20.7% 5-year figure cannot be read as the outcome of adjuvant gemcitabine in all comers. The paper does not flag this, and ESPAC-4's authors had to point it out

The primary endpoint was DISEASE-FREE SURVIVAL assessed in part by abdominal ultrasound every 8 weeks with no central radiology review and with recurrence dated from 'the first subjective symptom indicating relapse' - an unblinded, partly symptom-driven endpoint in an open-label trial, which is exactly the setting in which detection bias inflates a DFS difference. The 2.4-fold DFS difference (13.4 vs 6.7 months) sits oddly beside a 2.6-month median OS difference

OVERALL SURVIVAL WAS A SECONDARY ENDPOINT THAT BECAME SIGNIFICANT ONLY ON THE FINAL OF SEVERAL ANALYSES, nine years after the primary report; no multiplicity adjustment is reported for this repeated testing, and the paper presents P=.01 as if from a single prespecified analysis

NO CENTRAL PATHOLOGY REVIEW means R0/R1 and nodal status - two of the three stratification factors - were assigned locally across 88 centres with no uniform margin definition; the modern <=1 mm R1 definition was not in general use in 1998-2004, so the R1 subgroup (19% and 15%) is not comparable with later trials where R1 rates were 40-60%

The observation arm received predominantly gemcitabine at relapse, so the trial compares early with late gemcitabine; a pathway cannot cite it for the proposition that adjuvant chemotherapy adds survival over the same drug given at recurrence

The paper's own abstract reports median DFS in the observation arm as 6.7 months while the discussion quotes 6.9 months, and the discussion's comparison with JSAP-02 uses the latter - a small internal inconsistency in the headline number

Funding came in part from Lilly Germany, the manufacturer of gemcitabine, and one author was a former Eli Lilly employee holding Lilly stock. The sponsor is stated to have had no role, and statistical analysis was performed independently at Charite, but the drug being tested was the sponsor's product

Enrolment ran 1998-2004 with surgery performed to institutional standards; perioperative mortality, lymphadenectomy extent and imaging have all changed, so the 20.2-month observation-arm survival is not a usable benchmark for a contemporary pathway
24104372.n: 368 randomised, 354 eligible for intention-to-treat analysis (179 gemcitabine, 175 observation); 316 deaths (89.3%)
24104372.bottom_line: CONKO-001 established that six months of adjuvant gemcitabine after macroscopically complete resection improves disease-free survival (13.4 vs 6.7 months) and long-term overall survival (5-year 20.7% vs 10.4%) compared with observation, but in a population pre-selected for postoperative CA19-9 below 92.5 kU/L, with only a 2.6-month difference in median survival, and in a design that is effectively immediate versus delayed gemcitabine.
24104372.funding: Supported in part by a grant from Lilly Germany (manufacturer of gemcitabine), by the German Cancer Society (section AIO) and by a research grant from Charite-Universitaetsmedizin Berlin. Stated to be an investigator-initiated trial with Lilly having no role in design, conduct, analysis or publication; statistical analysis performed independently of the sponsor. Dr Oettle reports honoraria from Roche, Celgene and Fresenius; Dr Riess from nine companies; Dr Arning is a former Eli Lilly employee and owns Lilly stock.

limitations: Quality of life was NOT measured - stated explicitly as a limitation

The median survival in the combination arm was more than 3 months shorter than in the preceding phase 1-2 trial, which the authors attribute to that study having been conducted at only four US centres versus 151 centres in 11 countries here
Peripheral neuropathy was cumulative, though rapidly reversible in most patients with temporary discontinuation and dose reduction
The incremental risks of sepsis and pneumonitis required protocol amendments to increase awareness

Comparison with the FOLFIRINOX trial is complicated because that trial pooled phase 2 and 3 data, excluded patients over 75 and excluded ECOG 2, whereas 10% of MPACT patients were at least 75 and 8% had a poor performance status equivalent to ECOG 2
critique: COMPARATOR: single-agent gemcitabine, the standard of care when the trial was designed - appropriate at the time. But FOLFIRINOX had been published in May 2011, 11 months before MPACT closed accrual, and the trial continued against gemcitabine rather than amending; the two regimens were never compared head to head until NAPOLI 3 used a liposomal variant, so a decade of practice rested on cross-trial comparison

NON-RECEIPT OF ALLOCATED TREATMENT: 10/431 (2%) and 28/430 (7%) never received treatment (treated populations 421 and 402). The imbalance is in the control arm's favour direction-wise for ITT but means almost 7% of gemcitabine patients contributed only follow-up

GEMCITABINE DOSE WAS NOT EQUIVALENT BETWEEN ARMS. The combination arm received a median cumulative gemcitabine dose of 11,400 mg/m2 versus 9000 mg/m2 in the monotherapy arm because they stayed on treatment longer, and the control arm's cycle 1 used the different weekly-for-7-of-8-weeks schedule. Part of the observed benefit is therefore more gemcitabine, not nab-paclitaxel, and the trial cannot separate the two

A 1.8-MONTH MEDIAN GAIN IS SMALL IN ABSOLUTE TERMS and is routinely reported as 'increased survival' without it; the 2-year survival difference (9% vs 4%) involves roughly 20 extra patients alive out of 431

QUALITY OF LIFE WAS NEVER MEASURED, in a trial whose experimental arm caused 17% grade 3+ peripheral neuropathy and 17% grade 3+ fatigue versus 1% and 7%. PRODIGE 4, run in the same era, did measure it. A pathway choosing between nab-paclitaxel/gemcitabine and FOLFIRINOX has quality-of-life data for only one of them

THE NEUROPATHY RECOVERY DATA ARE REPORTED AMONG PATIENTS WHO IMPROVED and in medians of time to improvement, with no cumulative-incidence estimate of unresolved neuropathy at a fixed time point. APACT, the adjuvant trial of the same regimen, later found 84% of grade 3+ neuropathy had NOT improved to grade 1 or less at its primary cutoff - a far less reassuring picture of the same drug

THE SUBGROUP FINDING THAT THE SICKEST PATIENTS BENEFIT MOST is biologically plausible but is also what regression to the mean and differential early mortality in a poorly performing control arm would produce; no interaction tests are reported for these subgroups and they are presented in a forest plot without multiplicity adjustment

THE BILIRUBIN CEILING (at or below the upper limit of normal) IS STRICTER THAN PRODIGE 4's (1.5x normal) and excludes the jaundiced patients who make up a large share of real pancreatic head cancer, while the Karnofsky 70 floor admits frailer patients than PRODIGE 4 - so the two landmark metastatic trials selected differently in opposite directions on two different axes, and their medians (8.5 vs 11.1 months) cannot be compared

THE PHASE 1-2 RESULT (12.2 months) DID NOT REPLICATE, FALLING BY MORE THAN 3 MONTHS IN THE PHASE 3 TRIAL. The authors attribute this to multicentre generalisability, which is reasonable - but the same logic should be applied to every single-arm or few-centre pancreatic result quoted in a pathway, including the 24.2-month FOLFIRINOX figure for locally advanced disease

THE TRIAL WAS DESIGNED, MONITORED, SUPPLIED AND ANALYSED BY THE MANUFACTURER OF THE EXPERIMENTAL DRUG. The protocol was designed by the first author 'in collaboration with the sponsor' (Celgene), the sponsor monitored the study and provided drugs free, the biostatistician who analysed the data and vouches for its completeness is a Celgene employee and co-author, two authors are Celgene employees, and a sponsor-employed medical writer assisted. Comparing an expensive proprietary agent added to a generic backbone against that generic backbone alone is the comparator choice an industry sponsor has every reason to make
24131140.n: 861 patients (431 nab-paclitaxel plus gemcitabine, 430 gemcitabine); 823 treated; 692 deaths (80%)
24131140.bottom_line: MPACT established nab-paclitaxel plus gemcitabine as a first-line option in metastatic pancreatic cancer, improving median survival from 6.7 to 8.5 months (HR 0.72) with doubled 1- and 2-year survival in a population less restricted by age and performance status than the FOLFIRINOX trial - at the cost of 17% grade 3 neuropathy, with no quality-of-life data at all, with more cumulative gemcitabine in the experimental arm, and designed and analysed by the drug's manufacturer against a single-agent comparator.
24131140.funding: Celgene, the manufacturer of nab-paclitaxel (Abraxane). The sponsor monitored the study, provided the study drugs at no charge, and co-designed the protocol; clinical researchers and a biostatistician employed by Celgene are authors and the statistician vouches for the accuracy and completeness of the data; a sponsor-employed medical writer assisted with the manuscript.

limitations: The authors state the problem the template addresses — variability in expertise, variability in terminology defining disease extent, and incomplete documentation of findings — rather than limitations of the template itself
They note that imaging performance in defining resectability is imperfect, which is why standardised reporting is proposed
No stated limitations section for the consensus process itself
critique: A single consensus meeting in November 2011 with no Delphi process, no voting, no reported level of agreement and no grading of evidence behind any item; the only process described after the meeting is that the lead author prepared a draft and circulated it for comment and approval
No systematic literature review is described; items were chosen 'based on the state of knowledge and available pertinent literature', which is an unauditable basis

The 180-degree threshold that governs the borderline/unresectable boundary is adopted from existing NCCN criteria rather than derived or validated here, and no inter-reader reproducibility data for measuring circumferential contact are presented — yet the whole template rests on that measurement

No validation of any kind: the paper does not show that use of the template changes report completeness, inter-radiologist agreement, multidisciplinary decisions, resection rates or margins. It asserts that adoption 'should improve the decision-making process'

Published 2014 and referencing NCCN criteria of that era; resectability definitions have since diverged (anatomical versus the biological and conditional criteria of the later International Association of Pancreatology consensus), so a pathway citing this as current practice is citing a superseded anatomical-only framework
The paper makes no funding statement and does not describe conflict-of-interest management for the writing group; this cannot be verified from the extraction
A reporting template is a process intervention; quoting it as evidence for a resectability threshold conflates the lexicon with the evidence for where the threshold should sit
24354378.bottom_line: Provides the standardised vocabulary and reporting template that lets resectability be described consistently, including the 180-degree abutment/encasement rule, but it is expert consensus from a single 2011 meeting with no validation of reproducibility or of any effect on patient outcomes.

limitations: Non-optimal drugs were used because the study was designed in 2005, before FOLFIRINOX and nab-paclitaxel; more effective systemic treatment is needed
Although FOLFOX was suggested as second-line therapy in the protocol, subsequent lines of chemotherapy were not systematised
Quality-of-life and cost-efficacy analyses were not planned as secondary objectives
Assessment of pain was not optimal
Evaluation of tumour response and progression-free survival was NOT centralised

Survival in the second-randomisation population (15.2 and 16.5 months) was much higher than the hypothesised 9 and 12 months, which the authors attribute to induction chemotherapy selecting a more favourable prognostic group
Further intensification of the chemoradiotherapy regimen may be needed; IMRT and stereotactic body radiotherapy allow dose escalation not tested here
critique: COMPARATOR: continuation of the SAME gemcitabine-based chemotherapy for two more months. Neither arm received modern systemic therapy - the trial predates FOLFIRINOX and nab-paclitaxel as standards, and the authors concede the drugs were 'non-optimal'. A null result for radiotherapy added to gemcitabine does not establish that radiotherapy adds nothing to FOLFIRINOX, which is the question a contemporary pathway faces; CONKO-007 later asked that question and also found no survival benefit

NON-RECEIPT OF ALLOCATED TREATMENT: 12/133 (9%) allocated to chemoradiotherapy did not receive it and 4 more were unassessable for radiotherapy quality; in the first randomisation all 442 received their allocated induction. The larger loss is upstream: 173/442 (39%) never reached the second randomisation at all, so the primary comparison involves only 61% of the enrolled population

THE PRIMARY ENDPOINT IS MEASURED FROM THE FIRST RANDOMISATION BUT THE INTERVENTION IS ALLOCATED AT THE SECOND. Four months of survival are therefore common to both arms by construction, which dilutes any true effect of chemoradiotherapy toward the null and makes the 1.3-month difference even less informative than it looks. The preplanned sensitivity analysis from the second randomisation is mentioned in the methods but its result is not reported in the text for the primary comparison

THE TRIAL WAS STOPPED AT ITS INTERIM ANALYSIS FOR FUTILITY and that interim analysis was then declared the final one. It never reached its planned 392 deaths or 480-722 patients, so the confidence interval (0.79-1.34) cannot exclude a clinically meaningful 20% relative benefit or harm. 'No significant difference' here means underpowered, not equivalent

FIFTY PERCENT OF RADIOTHERAPY PLANS HAD MINOR AND 18% MAJOR PROTOCOL DEVIATIONS despite a formal quality assurance programme. The authors argue deviations did not significantly affect survival, but that analysis (17.0 vs 13.4 months, HR 1.43) is itself underpowered at 21 major-deviation patients and the point estimate runs in the harmful direction - so the trial cannot cleanly separate 'radiotherapy does not work' from 'this radiotherapy was not delivered well enough'

RESPONSE AND PROGRESSION WERE ASSESSED LOCALLY WITH NO CENTRAL REVIEW, in an open-label trial, which matters for the locoregional-versus-distant progression finding that is the paper's main positive claim: investigators who knew a patient had received abdominal radiotherapy were reading the same scans for local progression

THE SHIFT FROM LOCOREGIONAL (32% vs 46%) TO METASTATIC (60% vs 44%) PROGRESSION IS A COMPETING-RISK PHENOMENON reported as a treatment effect. Patients whose local disease is controlled live long enough to be recorded as progressing distantly; the paper does not analyse these as competing risks

BASELINE IMBALANCE AT THE SECOND RANDOMISATION FAVOURS NEITHER ARM CONSISTENTLY but is notable: 56% of the chemotherapy arm were men versus 44% of the chemoradiotherapy arm, and WHO performance status 1 was recorded in 25.3% versus 45.1% - a large imbalance in the paper's own Table 1 that is not commented on and would favour the chemotherapy arm
GRADE AND HISTOLOGIC DATA WERE UNKNOWN IN ABOUT HALF THE COHORT (50-53% 'unknown' grade), so the two arms cannot be shown comparable on a major prognostic variable

The 4% secondary resection rate is a genuinely important finding for a pathway - gemcitabine-based induction almost never converts locally advanced disease - but it is reported as a brief paragraph and contrasts with the 26% pooled resection rate Suker et al. report for FOLFIRINOX induction in the same year, a difference of regimen the trial could not test

The trial was supported by Roche, the manufacturer of erlotinib, one of the two interventions tested; the paper states Roche had no role in design, conduct, analysis or publication, and the erlotinib result was negative, which limits the concern
27139057.n: 442 eligible patients at first randomisation (223 gemcitabine, 219 gemcitabine-erlotinib); 269 at second randomisation (136 chemotherapy, 133 chemoradiotherapy); 379 deaths
27139057.bottom_line: LAP07 shows that consolidation chemoradiotherapy after four months of gemcitabine-based induction does not prolong survival in locally advanced pancreatic cancer (15.2 vs 16.5 months, HR 1.03) though it halves locoregional progression and roughly doubles treatment-free time, and that adding erlotinib to gemcitabine is useless and possibly harmful; it was stopped early for futility, used chemotherapy the authors themselves call obsolete, and achieved curative resection in only 4% of patients.

limitations: All included studies were non-randomised and most were retrospective, and retrospective studies are known to under-report toxicity - so the pooled adverse event rates are probably an underestimate
Progression-free survival may be biased because retrospective studies typically lack standardised on-treatment imaging

Studies used different definitions of locally advanced disease (NCCN in three, AHPBA/SSO/SSAT in three, multidisciplinary board or retrospective image review in seven); a consensus definition is needed

The included studies did NOT report how eligibility for FOLFIRINOX was determined, so it is unclear whether nearly all locally advanced patients or only the fittest subgroup received it - and therefore which patients can expect 24.2 months

After first-line FOLFIRINOX many patients had additional treatments (chemotherapy, targeted therapy, radiotherapy, resection) that varied within and across studies, with insufficient data to evaluate their effect on survival
No study reported standard pretreatment staging laparoscopy, which upstages up to a third of patients to metastatic disease in other reports; better staging might yield even longer survival
The favourable survival may be partly attributable to patient selection, and confirmation in a randomised trial is needed
critique: COMPARATOR: THERE IS NONE. The 24.2-month figure is compared only with a narrative range of '6-13 months' for gemcitabine drawn from two references, with no formal synthesis of the gemcitabine comparator and no adjustment for the different eras, staging and performance status of those cohorts. The paper is a single-arm pooled analysis presented with a historical benchmark

SELECTION, NOT DRUG EFFECT, IS THE MOST PARSIMONIOUS EXPLANATION AND THE AUTHORS CANNOT RULE IT OUT - they say so, but the headline figure is quoted everywhere without the caveat. FOLFIRINOX eligibility in 2011-2015 meant good performance status, normal bilirubin and age under about 76; the studies do not report their denominators, so the 24.2 months describes whoever was offered FOLFIRINOX, not patients with locally advanced disease

IMMORTAL TIME AND LEFT-TRUNCATION: survival is measured from the start of FOLFIRINOX, so every patient had to survive diagnosis, staging, biliary drainage and the decision to treat before entering the analysis. Patients who deteriorated or were found metastatic before chemotherapy could start are invisible. LAP07's 7.7-month median for patients who progressed during induction shows how large this excluded group is

ELEVEN OF THIRTEEN STUDIES ARE RETROSPECTIVE, AND NO STUDY USED STAGING LAPAROSCOPY. The authors argue this biases AGAINST FOLFIRINOX (occult metastatic patients included), but it cuts the other way for progression-free survival (no standardised imaging means later-detected progression) and the direction of net bias is unknowable

THREE-FOLD HETEROGENEITY IN THE PRIMARY OUTCOME (10.0 to 32.7 months) IS NOT FORMALLY QUANTIFIED. Because patient-level data were pooled into a single Kaplan-Meier curve rather than meta-analysed, no I2 or prediction interval is reported for overall survival - the headline estimate is presented with a narrow 95% CI (21.7-26.8) that reflects the number of patients, not the disagreement between studies. For the pooled proportions where I2 IS reported, it reaches 90%

THE 'LOCALLY ADVANCED' POPULATION IS NOT ONE POPULATION. Only three of thirteen studies enrolled exclusively locally advanced patients; the rest mixed in resectable, borderline resectable, metastatic and recurrent disease (355/689 locally advanced overall), and seven studies had no formal resectability criteria at all. Patients labelled locally advanced by a retrospective image review in 2011 would include patients a modern multidisciplinary board would call borderline resectable and resect

THE 25.9% RESECTION AND 78.4% R0 RATES ARE STUDY-LEVEL PROPORTIONS WITH I2 OF 24% AND 64% AND A PER-STUDY RANGE OF 0-43%, reflecting no consensus on who gets taken to surgery. The R0 denominator is resected patients only (81 of 325), so '78% R0' describes 19% of the cohort

NO DEATHS ATTRIBUTED TO FOLFIRINOX ACROSS 490 PATIENTS IS NOT CREDIBLE as a safety estimate from retrospective records; PRODIGE 4 recorded one treatment-related death in 171 patients prospectively. The authors acknowledge under-reporting but the figure is still presented as a finding

MANY OF THE CONTRIBUTING AUTHORS ARE THE INVESTIGATORS OF THE INCLUDED STUDIES, who supplied and 'checked' their own patient-level data. This is the standard way individual-patient meta-analyses are done and improves data quality, but it also means the included studies were not independently verified and no formal risk-of-bias judgement beyond a CASP score is reported per study

The comparison with ESPAC-3's adjuvant survival invites the inference that locally advanced disease treated with FOLFIRINOX does as well as resected disease - an inference between two differently selected populations that the paper then uses to motivate neoadjuvant FOLFIRINOX trials in resectable disease. NORPACT-1 and PREOPANC-2 subsequently failed to show that benefit
27160474.n: 13 studies, 689 patients, of whom 355 (52%) had locally advanced disease; 11 studies with 315 locally advanced patients contributed patient-level survival data
27160474.bottom_line: This individual-patient meta-analysis of 315 patients from 11 non-randomised studies is the source of the widely quoted 24.2-month median survival with FOLFIRINOX in locally advanced pancreatic cancer, and it shows resection is achieved in only about a quarter; because every study was non-randomised, most retrospective, none used staging laparoscopy and the per-study medians range from 10 to 33 months, the figure describes a selected and heterogeneous population and should be read as a hypothesis for the randomised trials it prompted, not as an expected outcome.

limitations: The paper carries no separate limitations section; the authors frame the pragmatic design (WHO 0-2, R1 margins, no CA19-9 ceiling) as a strength rather than discussing its downsides

The authors acknowledge that comparison with CONKO-001's better-looking gemcitabine survival must be read in the light of CONKO-001's CA19-9 ceiling, and that ESPAC-1's factorial design produced uncontrollable confounding
The authors note scepticism about the efficacy of the 5-fluorouracil and folinic acid regimens used in earlier ESPAC trials
Follow-up method (haematology, biochemistry, tumour marker use) was determined by each site because of wide variation in routine practice
critique: The paper has no limitations section at all, so almost everything below is unstated

COMPARATOR: adjuvant gemcitabine monotherapy, the then standard. This was a fair comparator in 2008-2014 but ESPAC-4's winner (gemcitabine plus capecitabine) was itself superseded 20 months later by adjuvant mFOLFIRINOX in PRODIGE-24 (median OS 54.4 months). A pathway should treat ESPAC-4 as establishing a fallback regimen for patients unfit for mFOLFIRINOX, not as current first choice

NON-RECEIPT OF ALLOCATED TREATMENT: only 7/730 (1%) never started, which is excellent, but 169/364 (46%) of combination patients and 127/366 (35%) of gemcitabine patients did not complete all six cycles, and the reason was UNKNOWN for 38 and 14 patients respectively. In an open-label trial reporting a 2.5-month median difference, 10% of the experimental arm stopping for unrecorded reasons is a real gap in the record

THE TRIAL WAS STOPPED AND PUBLISHED EARLY on the Independent Data and Safety Monitoring Committee's recommendation at 458 of 480 target deaths (95%), on 'a clear signal of efficacy'. Early stopping for benefit systematically overestimates effect size; Peto boundaries were used and no alpha adjustment was deemed necessary, but the point estimate should be read as an upper bound

THE PRIMARY ENDPOINT IS POSITIVE WHILE THE DISEASE-CONTROL ENDPOINT IS NOT. Relapse-free survival was not significantly different (HR 0.86, p=0.082) and median relapse-free survival differed by 0.8 months, yet 5-year overall survival differs by 12.5 percentage points. Either capecitabine acts after relapse, or the 5-year estimates - computed from a cohort with median follow-up of only 43.2 months and 51 patients lost to follow-up - are unstable. The widely quoted '28.8% vs 16.3% at 5 years' is an ESTIMATE extrapolated well past the bulk of the data and is not the trial's primary result

THE R0 SUBGROUP FINDING IS WHERE ALL THE BENEFIT SITS (39.5 vs 27.9 months in R0; 23.7 vs 23.0 months in R1) BUT 60% OF THE TRIAL WAS R1. No interaction test is reported for treatment-by-margin; a trend test across four groups is given instead. A pathway reading ESPAC-4 as supporting adjuvant GemCap for margin-positive patients is reading something the data do not show

EIGHT PATIENTS WITH STAGE IV DISEASE WERE ENROLLED 'because they were anxious to join the trial' and retained in the analysis, along with patients whose postoperative CA19-9 was unmeasured (68 patients, 9%). These are small numbers but represent protocol deviations accepted post hoc

The 2.5-month median difference comes at the cost of substantially more grade 3-4 neutropenia (38% vs 24%), diarrhoea and hand-foot syndrome, with 46% of the combination arm failing to complete treatment - a benefit-harm balance the paper's 'without any significant increase in overall toxicity' framing understates
Only 35-39% of relapsing patients received any treatment at relapse, far below the 93% in PRODIGE-24; the survival curves therefore reflect an era and a setting with limited salvage therapy

Open-label design with no central pathology or radiology review; the R0 definition used was the strict <=1 mm Royal College of Pathologists standard, which is correct but makes the R0 rate (40%) incomparable with trials using older definitions

The senior author reports grants from seven companies, paid consultancy from four and lecture fees from two; the trial itself was funded by Cancer Research UK with no industry role, and capecitabine is generic, so commercial influence on the comparator is unlikely
28129987.n: 732 randomised, 730 analysed (366 gemcitabine, 364 gemcitabine plus capecitabine); 458 deaths (95% of the 480-death target)
28129987.bottom_line: ESPAC-4 established adjuvant gemcitabine plus capecitabine over gemcitabine alone in an unusually unselected resected population (median OS 28.0 vs 25.5 months, HR 0.82; estimated 5-year 28.8% vs 16.3%), but the relapse-free survival endpoint was negative, the benefit is concentrated in R0 patients, the trial was stopped early for benefit, and its winner has since been displaced by adjuvant mFOLFIRINOX in fit patients.

limitations: Public reference controls, not study-recruited controls, were used to estimate background mutation prevalence; the authors argue extensive filtering normalised the two data sets and that ExAC and gnomAD gave concordant results
The 21-gene panel does not cover all possible predisposition genes, so other contributing genes may have been missed
A number of variants of uncertain significance could not be classified as deleterious or neutral
Cases came from three Mayo Clinic sites and were younger and less likely to be Black or Hispanic than SEER pancreatic cancer patients, so generalisability may be limited
The study had insufficient information to estimate penetrance (lifetime cancer probability) in carriers
critique: Case-control comparison against sequencing databases assembled for other purposes is vulnerable to differential variant-calling and coverage between cases and controls; the authors address data cleaning but not platform-level batch effects, and the very wide CIs for CDKN2A (5.43-25.61) and MLH1 (1.94-17.53) rest on a handful of carriers each

The headline 5.5% figure is driven mostly by ATM and BRCA2; a pathway that quotes '5.5% carry an actionable germline mutation' is conflating genes with established therapeutic consequences (BRCA1/2, and by extension PALB2) with genes that have none in pancreatic cancer (CDKN2A, TP53)

A clinic-based case series at a tertiary referral centre over 16 years oversamples patients who survived long enough to be enrolled and consented; the null survival association (HR 0.86) is therefore not a clean test of whether carriage affects prognosis

Multiplicity across 21 genes and several subgroup strata (family history, age, race) is not formally controlled, and the authors report subgroup ORs for family-history strata as if independently estimated

Two co-authors were employees of Qiagen, which supplies variant-interpretation software, a relationship relevant to how variants were classified; the paper discloses this but does not discuss its bearing on classification
The paper establishes risk association only; it supports cascade testing of relatives but says nothing about whether testing changes outcomes, which is the claim a pathway page usually wants to make
29922827.n: 3030 pancreatic adenocarcinoma cases with germline sequencing (123 136 reference controls)
29922827.bottom_line: Establishes that deleterious germline mutations in six genes are over-represented in unselected pancreatic cancer and are present in 5.5% of patients regardless of family history, but does not establish penetrance, does not show that carriage affects survival, and does not make most of those six genes therapeutically actionable.

Thompson Charitable Fund; funders stated to have had no role in design, conduct or analysis

limitations: The data were acknowledged as immature at this analysis, with 61% of all patients still alive

The authors note that the unusually long overall survival in the gemcitabine arm (35.0 months versus 20.1-26.5 months in previous trials) may be due to the high use of FOLFIRINOX after relapse in that arm (76% of patients)

Disease-free survival is not validated as a surrogate endpoint for overall survival in adjuvant pancreatic trials; it was chosen for earlier assessment and fewer patients, and the authors argue it correlated with overall survival here

Eligibility required patients fit enough for modified FOLFIRINOX, a postoperative CT or MRI and a postoperative CA 19-9 below 180 U/mL in order to minimise inclusion of occult metastatic disease - the authors present this as quality control
The database was locked early (April 2018) on the data and safety monitoring committee's recommendation for ethical reasons at 91.8% of expected DFS events
critique: COMPARATOR: adjuvant gemcitabine monotherapy. By the time this trial reported, ESPAC-4 (published January 2017) had already shown gemcitabine plus capecitabine superior to gemcitabine. PRODIGE-24 therefore never tested mFOLFIRINOX against the best available comparator, and the 19.4-month median survival gain is measured against a regimen already known to be inferior to an easier combination

THE 54.4-MONTH MEDIAN SURVIVAL IS THE SINGLE MOST MISUSED NUMBER IN PANCREATIC ONCOLOGY AND APPLIES TO A HEAVILY PRE-SELECTED POPULATION. Patients had to be 79 or younger, free of coronary disease, WHO 0-1, fully recovered from surgery, with a clear postoperative scan AND a postoperative CA19-9 below 180 U/mL. ESPAC-4 showed that excluding CA19-9 above 92.5 kU/L alone removes a group whose median survival is 13.1 months. Neoadjuvant trials randomise at diagnosis and cannot be compared with this number, and a pathway that quotes 54.4 months as the expectation for resected PDAC is quoting the outcome of the fittest fifth of the disease

NON-RECEIPT OF ALLOCATED TREATMENT: 9/247 (3.6%) in the mFOLFIRINOX arm (6 withdrew consent, 2 metastatic, 1 physician withdrawal) and 3/246 (1.2%) in the gemcitabine arm never received the drug - low and reasonably balanced. The larger issue is incomplete delivery: only 66% completed all 12 mFOLFIRINOX cycles and fewer than half achieved a relative dose intensity of 0.70
FIFTEEN PATIENTS (9 AND 6) HAD MAJOR ELIGIBILITY VIOLATIONS, MOSTLY OCCULT METASTATIC DISEASE (8 and 5), and 13 patients were stage IV at baseline; they remain in the intention-to-treat population

THE PRIMARY ENDPOINT WAS DISEASE-FREE SURVIVAL, WHICH THE AUTHORS CONCEDE IS NOT A VALIDATED SURROGATE, assessed without blinded central radiology review in an open-label trial. The APACT trial later showed that independent blinded review and investigator assessment of recurrence in this setting diverge substantially (18.8 vs 13.7 months in the same gemcitabine arm), which means an open-label DFS endpoint in pancreatic adjuvant trials is genuinely fragile

THE TRIAL WAS STOPPED EARLY FOR EFFICACY at 91.8% of expected events, which inflates the effect estimate; the 5-year report (Conroy 2022) duly shows attenuation (DFS HR 0.58 to 0.66, OS HR 0.64 to 0.68, median OS 54.4 to 53.5 months)

ASYMMETRIC CROSSOVER AT RELAPSE CUTS BOTH WAYS AND IS NOT ADDRESSED. Seventy-six percent of relapsing gemcitabine patients received FOLFIRINOX, which the authors invoke to explain the unusually good 35-month control arm - but this means the trial measures the benefit of GIVING mFOLFIRINOX EARLY rather than at relapse, not the benefit of the drug itself. The same logic the authors apply to the control arm undermines the magnitude of the headline difference

BASELINE IMBALANCE IN LYMPHOVASCULAR INVASION FAVOURED THE CONTROL ARM (73.7% in mFOLFIRINOX vs 63.1% in gemcitabine, P=0.02) - the only significant baseline difference, and it runs against the experimental arm, so it does not explain the result

G-CSF WAS GIVEN TO 62% OF mFOLFIRINOX PATIENTS AND 3.7% OF GEMCITABINE PATIENTS. The regimens were not supported equally, which matters for any claim that neutropenia rates were 'similar' between arms

THE REGIMEN DELIVERED IS NOT THE REGIMEN NAMED. Irinotecan was cut from 180 to 150 mg/m2 mid-trial, bolus fluorouracil was omitted from the start, and 34% of patients never completed 12 cycles; 'adjuvant mFOLFIRINOX' in practice means a dose-attenuated, incompletely delivered regimen

In routine practice up to 30% of resected patients never start adjuvant chemotherapy at all; this trial randomised only those who had already recovered, so it quantifies the benefit conditional on reaching that point and not the benefit of a surgery-first strategy

R&D Unicancer, a co-sponsor, received a grant from Chugai Pharmaceutical, employed two of the authors, collected and analysed the data and funded the editorial and writing assistance; Sanofi-Aventis Canada supplied oxaliplatin. Nearly every clinical author declares industry payments. The drugs are generic, which limits commercial motive, but the sponsor controlled the data and the write-up
30575490.n: 493 patients (247 modified FOLFIRINOX, 246 gemcitabine); 314 disease-free survival events (91.8% of target) and 192 deaths at this analysis
30575490.bottom_line: PRODIGE-24 established adjuvant modified FOLFIRINOX as the standard for fit patients after resection, nearly doubling median disease-free survival (21.6 vs 12.8 months) and adding 19.4 months of median overall survival over gemcitabine at the cost of 76% grade 3-4 toxicity - but in a population selected for age under 80, no cardiac disease, full surgical recovery and postoperative CA19-9 below 180 U/mL, against an already-outdated comparator, with heavy FOLFIRINOX crossover in the control arm and early stopping for benefit.

Oxaliplatin was supplied to Canadian centres by Sanofi-Aventis Canada, stated to have had no role. limitations: Overall survival was reported at an interim analysis with only 46% data maturity and showed no significant difference

Overall survival may be confounded by subsequent therapy, including the nine placebo patients (15%) who received a PARP inhibitor after progression, and by placebo-group patients going on to further DNA-damaging agents
Placebo rather than continued chemotherapy was chosen as comparator on the grounds that cumulative neuropathy and other toxicity limit extended platinum therapy

The trial used dual selection — germline BRCA mutation plus no progression on at least 16 weeks of platinum — so the population is enriched for benefit; of 3315 screened, 7.5% had a germline BRCA mutation
Time to second progression is an endpoint without precedent in pancreatic cancer and was interpreted by analogy with other tumour types
critique: COMPARATOR: placebo, not maintenance chemotherapy or a de-escalated fluoropyrimidine. The trial therefore establishes that olaparib beats stopping treatment, not that it beats continuing anything, which is the comparison a pathway actually faces at the 16-week mark

The 3315-to-154 funnel (4.6% of screened patients randomised) means the result applies to a population that must be found by population-wide germline testing plus four months of platinum response — a conditioning step that is itself the strongest prognostic selection in the trial

PFS is the only positive endpoint and it is a progression-imaging endpoint in an unblinded-to-progression-pattern disease; the paper does not report sensitivity analyses for differential assessment timing or informative censoring, and the alpha spent on PFS leaves overall survival with no formal success criterion in this report

A median OS of 18.1 months in the placebo arm of metastatic pancreatic cancer is far above the 6-11 months typical of the disease, confirming how selected this population is; quoting POLO alongside unselected trials is not like-for-like
Grade 3+ toxicity nearly doubled (40% vs 23%) for a benefit confined to an imaging endpoint with no survival or quality-of-life gain — the harm half of the ledger is quantified but not weighed

AstraZeneca (in alliance with Merck Sharp & Dohme) funded the trial, supplied the companion diagnostic pathway (BRACAnalysis CDx, Myriad) and provided sponsor-funded medical writing; the choice of placebo over active maintenance is the design decision most favourable to the sponsor and is defended in one sentence

Nine placebo patients crossing to a PARP inhibitor is cited as biasing OS towards the null, but the direction is asserted rather than quantified, and no sensitivity analysis censoring at crossover is presented
31157963.bottom_line: In the 4.6% of screened patients who have a germline BRCA mutation and have already not progressed on four months of platinum, maintenance olaparib delays radiographic progression by 3.6 months against placebo, but does not improve overall survival or quality of life at this analysis and has not been tested against continued chemotherapy.

limitations: Median OS in the immediate surgery arm was better than the 11 months assumed when powering the trial (14.3 months), so the trial was underpowered for its design
A 24% dropout rate in the chemoradiotherapy arm before starting treatment, including 10 patients whose treatment was delayed by persistent jaundice after biliary drainage
Fourteen patients (6%) had pathology other than PDAC, 9 cholangiocarcinoma, with a more favourable prognosis
The authors state the resectable-versus-borderline difference must be interpreted cautiously because the interaction test was not significant
Comparison with contemporary adjuvant trials (ESPAC-4, PRODIGE-24) is acknowledged as difficult because adjuvant trials exclude patients who progress or do not recover from surgery
critique: COMPARATOR: the control arm was upfront surgery followed by six cycles of adjuvant GEMCITABINE MONOTHERAPY. This was Dutch standard of care when the trial was designed but was superseded during the trial by ESPAC-4 (gemcitabine/capecitabine, 2017) and PRODIGE-24 (mFOLFIRINOX, 2018). The control arm therefore did NOT receive modern adjuvant therapy, and the trial cannot support a claim about neoadjuvant therapy versus current standard upfront treatment

NON-RECEIPT OF ALLOCATED TREATMENT: 28/119 (24%) allocated to chemoradiotherapy never started it (13 metastatic at staging laparoscopy, 4 progressed, 3 crossed to urgent surgery, 3 died, plus protocol violations), and 7 crossed over to surgery without neoadjuvant treatment. In the surgery arm 6/127 (5%) never had surgery and only 65/127 (51%) ever received any chemotherapy. Roughly a quarter of each arm did not receive the strategy it was assigned

The paper's conclusion and the widely quoted 35.2-vs-19.8-month figure rest on a NEGATIVE primary endpoint plus a subgroup of patients selected by surviving to resection and tolerating adjuvant therapy - a post-randomisation selection that cannot be read as a randomised comparison; a pathway should not cite it as the effect of neoadjuvant therapy

The experimental arm underwent mandatory staging laparoscopy (114/119) while laparoscopy was discretionary in the surgery arm, so occult metastatic disease was systematically removed from the neoadjuvant arm's resection denominator earlier and more reliably - a selection asymmetry that inflates the R0 and nodal comparisons

R0 rate is reported per resected patient (71% of 72) rather than per randomised patient, which flatters the arm with the lower resection rate; by ITT the R0 difference is much smaller (41% vs 28%, as reported in the 2022 long-term paper)
The regimen bundles chemotherapy with radiotherapy, so no inference about the contribution of radiotherapy is possible; the trial also used gemcitabine, not a multi-agent neoadjuvant regimen
Dutch resectability criteria are narrower than NCCN criteria, so a subset of NCCN borderline resectable patients was never eligible, limiting transportability of the borderline subgroup finding
Open-label design with no central radiology or pathology review reported for the primary analysis
Baseline imbalance in WHO performance status (58% PS 0 in the neoadjuvant arm vs 39% in the surgery arm) favours the experimental arm and is not adjusted for in the primary analysis
32105518.n: 246 eligible patients (119 preoperative chemoradiotherapy, 127 immediate surgery); 164 resections
32105518.bottom_line: PREOPANC's primary analysis did NOT show a survival benefit for neoadjuvant gemcitabine-based chemoradiotherapy over immediate surgery (16.0 vs 14.3 months, P=.096); it establishes better margin, nodal and locoregional outcomes and better treatment delivery, against an adjuvant gemcitabine comparator that is no longer standard, and the quoted large survival gains come from subgroups selected after randomisation.

limitations: The study was not designed or powered for a between-arm comparison, so the similarity of the two regimens is descriptive only
The marked difficulty in delineating resectability is a limitation of the trial's own population definition: 29% of enrolled patients did not meet radiologic criteria on central review
Central radiology review was retrospective rather than real time, so ineligible patients were not identified before treatment and enrolling sites were not notified
Pathologic assessments were performed locally rather than centrally
Prophylactic growth factor support was not allowed at treatment initiation, which may have affected tolerability
Tumour markers were not followed and were not used for patient selection or treatment decisions, unlike the adjuvant trials used as the historical comparator
The trial was not intended as an adjuvant-versus-neoadjuvant comparison, and radiation was not used
critique: COMPARATOR: THERE IS NO CONTROL ARM. Both arms were compared with a HISTORICAL 2-year survival of 40% taken from adjuvant trials. The authors themselves point out that adjuvant trial populations are highly selected - patients who did not progress before resection, had no intraoperative metastases, recovered to performance status 0-1 and, in PRODIGE-24, were further selected by postoperative CA19-9. Comparing a cohort randomised at diagnosis with a cohort randomised after successful recovery from surgery biases against the perioperative strategy, and the trial's 'failure' to beat 40% should not be read as perioperative chemotherapy being inferior

NO MODERN ADJUVANT THERAPY COMPARATOR EXISTS IN THIS TRIAL AT ALL: the postoperative component was simply a continuation of the same perioperative regimen (6 more doses of mFOLFIRINOX or 9 more of gemcitabine/nab-paclitaxel), reached by only 56% and 55% of eligible patients and completed by 49% and 40%. Nobody in this trial received upfront surgery followed by adjuvant mFOLFIRINOX

NON-RECEIPT OF ALLOCATED TREATMENT: 2/55 and 2/47 of eligible patients never started preoperative chemotherapy, and 1 patient withdrew consent before any therapy and was deemed non-evaluable. The larger problem is upstream: 45 of 147 randomised patients (31%) were removed from the analysed population - 43 for failing central radiology review and 1 for an incorrect primary tumour - even though all of them received protocol therapy. The reported denominators are therefore a centrally adjudicated subset of the randomised cohort, which is a selection step applied after randomisation

THE 29% CENTRAL-REVIEW INELIGIBILITY RATE IS THE MOST IMPORTANT FINDING FOR A PATHWAY AND IS BURIED AS A SECONDARY OBSERVATION. Over half the ineligible patients had arterial interface and nearly two thirds had suspicion of distant disease, meaning that in real-world multidisciplinary practice across 20-plus experienced centres, roughly a third of patients called resectable were not. Any pathway that assigns treatment by resectability category must account for this misclassification rate, and the trial shows a site-level checklist barely improves it
AGE WAS CAPPED AT 75 AND PERFORMANCE STATUS AT ZUBROD 0-1, so the population is substantially fitter than the patients a pathway will see; the median age was 64-66

The 85% R0 rate and 25-42% pathologic response rates are reported in a RESECTED-ONLY denominator (40 and 33 patients) that excludes the 27-30% who never reached surgery because of toxicity, deterioration or progression

Pathologic response was graded locally with no central review, and the numerically higher major response rate with gemcitabine/nab-paclitaxel (42% vs 25%) sits oddly beside its identical survival - an inconsistency the authors acknowledge but which also undercuts pathologic response as a surrogate

Enrolment was halted and the sample size expanded mid-trial in response to the ineligibility rate, and the study reopened with a revised protocol - a design change made with knowledge of accumulating data
The two regimens differ in scheduled dose density and in growth factor policy, so 'equally toxic' and 'equally effective' conclusions rest on a comparison the design forbids and on 102 patients
Several authors declare industry relationships including with Celgene, the manufacturer of nab-paclitaxel, one of the two tested regimens
33475684.n: 147 enrolled; 102 eligible and evaluable (55 mFOLFIRINOX, 47 gemcitabine/nab-paclitaxel); 73 resections. 43 of 146 reviewed (29%) were ineligible on central radiology review
33475684.bottom_line: S1505 shows that perioperative mFOLFIRINOX and gemcitabine plus nab-paclitaxel are deliverable in resectable PDAC with 70-73% resection rates and 85% R0 rates but produce only about 23 months median and 47-48% 2-year survival, neither arm beating a historical adjuvant-trial benchmark of 40%; it has no randomised control, excludes 31% of enrolled patients from its analysis, and its most durable contribution is the demonstration that 29% of patients called resectable by their own centres were not.

Several authors report personal fees from Celgene, Perthera, Incyte, Ability Pharma, AstraZeneca, Merck, Array, Ipsen, HUYA and Rafael, and institutional grants from numerous companies.

limitations: Only 3 of 17 included studies were randomised, which the authors say may threaten the authenticity of the review
Patient characteristics, tumour grade, drug administration protocols and control groups varied across included studies despite no significant measured heterogeneity
Multiple outcomes and insufficient studies made more detailed subgroup analysis difficult

limitations: Retrospective analysis in which the decision-making process and intent of the surgeons is unknown
Uncontrolled selection bias limits the generalisability of the reported outcomes
The NCDB lacks any information on primary or metastatic tumour RESECTABILITY
No granular data on the type of liver resection, or the number, location and size of metastatic tumours
Inherent NCDB limitations from missing or incomplete data including CA19-9 and the exact chemotherapy regimen and timing
Hepatectomy margin status is not recorded in the database and so could not be included in the Cox model
The authors conclude surgery for stage IV PDAC should be performed only within a well-designed prospective clinical trial
critique: COMPARATOR: patients who received chemotherapy alone, matched on SIX variables - age, sex, race, comorbidity, primary tumour site and tumour size. NONE of the variables that actually drive the decision to operate were matched: number or size of liver metastases, response to chemotherapy, CA 19-9 trajectory, performance status, or duration of pre-surgical treatment. Propensity matching on demographics while omitting response to therapy does not remove confounding, it conceals it, and the paper's own Table II shows the surgical group was younger, better differentiated, lower CA19-9 and 47 times more likely to have had chemotherapy

IMMORTAL TIME BIAS IS UNADDRESSED AND LARGE. Patients must survive diagnosis, staging and (in those who had it) months of chemotherapy to reach pancreatectomy, while the comparison group's clock starts at diagnosis. Kaslow et al., in the same literature, show that applying a 12-month landmark to a liver-only metastatic cohort raises median survival from 9 to 26 months with no surgery at all - larger than the 7.5-month difference this paper attributes to resection. No landmark analysis was performed here

THE PROPENSITY-MATCHED COHORT IS 137 SURGICAL PATIENTS matched to 137 of 25,268 chemotherapy patients, drawn from 1:1 nearest-neighbour matching on a treatment with a 0.29% prevalence. With that degree of imbalance, the matched controls are the extreme tail of the propensity distribution and residual confounding by unmeasured indication is near-certain

THE 15.6-MONTH FIGURE IS SELECTED FROM THE MOST FAVOURABLE OF SEVERAL ANALYSES. The whole surgical cohort achieved 10.74 months; the 137 who had both organs resected and were matched achieved 15.6 months. The authors themselves point out that 10.74 months is no better than chemotherapy alone in unselected metastatic disease, which is the more honest summary of the national experience

EIGHTY-FIVE PERCENT OF THE SURGICAL COHORT HAD THE PRIMARY RESECTED WITHOUT THE LIVER METASTASES, AND ONLY 13.5% HAD PREOPERATIVE CHEMOTHERAPY. The authors suspect many were incidental occult metastases found at exploration, where guidelines say the operation should be abandoned. This means the national dataset is substantially capturing a practice error, not the carefully selected conversion surgery that the expert series describe - and yet the survival signal is attributed to the strategy

NO INFORMATION ON RESECTABILITY, METASTASIS NUMBER, SIZE OR MARGIN STATUS, in a study whose entire question is whether resecting oligometastatic disease helps. 'Oligometastatic' appears in the title but cannot be operationalised in the NCDB at all

SURGEON AND CENTRE VOLUME WERE THE STRONGEST PREDICTORS OF UNDERGOING SURGERY (surgeon volume OR 2.65) AND ARE ALSO STRONG PREDICTORS OF SURVIVAL, so the treatment effect is partly a centre effect. High hospital volume was entered in the Cox model and was null (HR 0.99), but surgeon volume was not

THE COX MODEL FOR SURVIVAL (Table IV) PRODUCES AN IMPLAUSIBLE RESULT - well-to-moderately differentiated tumours have HR 4.09 (2.32-7.23) for death, the opposite of the known direction and of the paper's own logistic model - which suggests a coding or reference-category problem in the adjusted analysis that underlies the HR 0.5 headline

CA 19-9 IS REPORTED AS '67 vs 77.6 U/mL' with a standard deviation of 39.9, and the baseline table dichotomises it at 98 U/mL with 92% of patients above that threshold. These numbers are not internally coherent and the variable is effectively unusable, yet it is cited as evidence that the surgical group had more favourable biology

The paper's conclusion ('may be associated with improved survival in well-selected patients ... should only be performed under a well-designed prospective clinical trial') is appropriately cautious, but the abstract's propensity-matched figure is what gets quoted

Future work is needed to identify criteria selecting patients who will benefit from local therapies including radiotherapy and surgery

critique: COMPARATOR: THE TRIAL HAS NO RANDOMISED CONTROL ARM FOR ITS PRIMARY QUESTION. Each arm was tested against a HISTORICAL 18-month survival rate of 50%, derived by the investigators from a literature review of studies published 2004-2015 and set at the lower bound of the IQR. Any claim that mFOLFIRINOX improves survival rests on a benchmark assembled from pre-FOLFIRINOX-era observational series with different staging and imaging, not on a contemporaneous control

NON-RECEIPT OF ALLOCATED TREATMENT: 5/70 (7%) randomised to arm 1 and 1/56 (2%) to arm 2 never initiated the intervention and were EXCLUDED from analysis entirely; the denominators of 65 and 55 are 'evaluable patients who initiated treatment', not randomised patients. This is a per-protocol-style analysis, not intention to treat, and excluding the 5 who withdrew or progressed before starting removes patients with worse prognosis. In addition 15/55 (27%) of arm 2 patients never received the radiotherapy that defines their arm

ARM 1 IS NOT A PURELY RANDOMISED COHORT: 16 of its 70 patients were sequentially registered WITHOUT randomisation after arm 2 closed. Nearly a quarter of the arm that 'won' was enrolled non-randomly, in a later calendar period, with knowledge of the interim R0 results

THE ARM 2 FUTILITY RULE WAS BASED ON R0 RESECTION RATE, A SURROGATE, IN THE FIRST 30 PATIENTS. The trial then reports median OS of 17.1 vs 29.8 months as if radiotherapy were harmful, when the design explicitly forbids that comparison and arm 2 was stopped on a surrogate before its survival data matured. The paper's own conclusion that mFOLFIRINOX 'was associated with favorable OS compared with mFOLFIRINOX plus radiotherapy' is a comparison the statistical plan does not license

THE 18-MONTH OS RATES OF 87.5% AND 78.9% QUOTED FOR RESECTED PATIENTS USE A DENOMINATOR THAT EXCLUDES EVERYONE WHO PROGRESSED, DETERIORATED OR DIED BEFORE SURGERY - exactly the patients who did badly. Only 49% and 35% of evaluable patients reached pancreatectomy, so these figures describe the best half of the cohort and must not be quoted as outcomes of the regimen

The primary endpoint was a BINARY 18-month survival proportion tested at a ONE-SIDED alpha of 0.07 with 82% power - a deliberately permissive threshold. The trial is a screening study for further investigation, not a definitive efficacy trial, yet it is routinely cited as establishing mFOLFIRINOX as the 'reference regimen'

Only one of the two pathologic complete responses could be confirmed on central re-review of the pretreatment cytology; the other patient's slides were unavailable, leaving open the possibility that the specimen never contained adenocarcinoma

Radiotherapy was heterogeneous: two different techniques at two very different doses (33-40 Gy in 5 fractions versus 25 Gy in 5 fractions), with 12.5% of treated patients receiving the lower-dose HIGRT, so a null radiotherapy result may reflect an undertreated subset

Multiple investigators, including the senior author, report extensive industry relationships, and one radiotherapy co-author reports personal fees and grants from a radiotherapy device manufacturer (ViewRay) - relevant to a trial adjudicating the value of radiotherapy

Despite an upper age limit of 80, only 20.5% of patients were 70 or older, while increasing numbers of older patients are now being considered for resection and adjuvant chemotherapy

Most patients in both arms relapse, and mFOLFIRINOX delays rather than prevents recurrence in the large majority; a 7-point difference in 5-year DFS alongside an 11.8-point difference in 5-year OS implies part of the survival gain accrues after relapse, which is hard to attribute to the adjuvant regimen

Patients who have already had four months of mFOLFIRINOX have fewer options and more residual neuropathy at relapse; the trial does not weigh this against the upfront gain, and 93% of the whole cohort received relapse treatment, far above real-world rates

THE RECURRENCE-PATTERN FINDING IS UNADJUSTED AND CIRCULAR. More lung-only recurrence in the mFOLFIRINOX arm is reported as a favourable shift, but lung-only recurrence both occurs later and carries better prognosis, so patients who survive longer on more effective therapy have more opportunity to present with it. This is competing-risk confounding reported as a biological effect

THE PROGNOSTIC MODELLING IS ENTIRELY POST HOC with variables selected by stepwise procedures at P<.20 and no correction for multiplicity, yet 'larger-volume center' is presented as a novel finding. Centre volume in a trial of 77 hospitals is confounded with case mix, surgical quality, access to relapse therapy and country, none of which is adjusted for

THE LANDMARK ANALYSIS OF TREATMENT COMPLETION IS A CLASSIC HEALTHY-ADHERER COMPARISON. Patients who complete all cycles are those who did not relapse, deteriorate or become toxic during treatment; the 8-month landmark reduces but does not remove this, and the authors' own finding that DOSE INTENSITY did NOT predict survival (HR 1.01) is the clue that completion is marking patient fitness rather than drug effect. Presenting completion as a predictor invites the inference that pushing patients through all 12 cycles improves survival, which these data cannot support

ONLY 20.5% OF PATIENTS WERE 70 OR OLDER AND THE AGE-70 SUBGROUP SHOWED NO SIGNIFICANT BENEFIT in the primary report (HR 0.86 for DFS); the multivariable model here identifies age under 70 as an independent favourable factor. A pathway applying mFOLFIRINOX to a median-age PDAC population (around 70) is extrapolating

The cross-trial table comparing 5-year survival across CONKO-001, ESPAC-3/4, JASPAC-01, APACT and PRODIGE-24 is presented without adjustment for the very different CA19-9 ceilings, age limits and salvage-therapy rates the authors elsewhere identify as decisive, inviting exactly the naive cross-trial comparison the paper warns against for neoadjuvant trials

Safety is not re-analysed ('no new safety signals'), so the long-term neuropathy and quality-of-life cost of 12 cycles of mFOLFIRINOX remains unquantified at 5 years - and quality of life was never collected
